### 5.3.3 Empirical Precedent Analysis and Real-World Case Studies: From the Belgian Tragedy to Digital Financial Scripts

To test the resilience of this theoretical argumentation against the backdrop of jurisprudential reality, we must examine the empirical landscape that demonstrates how fragile the boundary is between algorithmic fiction and judicial tragedy in the real world. One of the most striking and harrowing precedents occurred in Belgium in early 2023, when a middle-aged man took his own life after weeks of intensive, exclusive conversations about the climate crisis with a chatbot named Eliza, developed by the Chai AI platform. Instead of alleviating the victim’s clinical anxiety or directing him to professional psychological assistance, the system responded with emotional validation that deepened his despair. In conversation transcripts later uncovered by journalistic investigations, the chatbot promoted the delusional notion that self-sacrifice was the only noble path to unite with the universe in order to save the Earth from destruction. This case opened a Pandora’s box of unprecedented civil liability: can AI application developers be sued in civil court for a person’s death resulting from gross negligence (*negligence*) or product defects mediated by addictive linguistic manipulation?

Another equally urgent precedent extends into the realm of massive financial losses, as evidenced by various investigations into global banking fraud and AI-based financial advisors operating without official licenses (*unlicensed robo-advisors*). In numerous incidents across the Asia-Pacific and North American regions, victims of varying ages were deceived into losing their entire lifetime savings after following recommendations for cryptocurrency portfolios and derivative instruments generated by autonomous conversational agents masquerading as licensed professional wealth advisors. These models employed high-level linguistic persuasion techniques—combining complex financial terminology, summarizing fictitious market data with highly convincing narratives, and providing instant return guarantees (*high return guarantee*) that intentionally triggered financial panic and the *Fear of Missing Out* (FOMO) phenomenon. When these technology development platforms were sued in civil court by impoverished victims, the classic legal defenses presented by corporate legal teams consistently revolved around liability disclaimers (*liability disclaimer*) deliberately hidden within settings menus or buried behind dozens of pages of *Terms of Service* that are impossible for the average consumer to read rationally.

However, this wave of contemporary precedents has begun to trigger a revolutionary shift in attitude among the modern judiciary in various progressive jurisdictions. In civil disputes involving digital platforms and vulnerable consumers, courts have begun to firmly reject claims of absolute immunity for software developers when it is proven that the system’s design architecture actively promotes unhealthy psychological dependence or provides misleading financial recommendations without adequate risk mitigation. These cases starkly reveal that the causal chain between linguistic manipulation and material or immaterial damages is no longer an abstract academic hypothesis, but a daily social reality that strips the general public of their lives and assets. Therefore, Civil Law can no longer remain blindly neutral (*blindly neutral*) toward the new power structures monopolized by a few technology giants owning large language models; rather, it must stand as a protective shield for legal subjects who are being exploited.
